lessons.title: দ্বিতীয় (ditiyô) — second, and the second layer it comes from
lessons.gloss: second — the word chapter twelve promised you without naming it, and a cluster that is on the page but not in the mouth

segments.text: A second kind of number word starts here, so the recalls come first, at the three growing distances this book can measure.

segments.instruction: write থ — R2, five lessons back
say he, she — R3, twenty lessons back

segments.text: দ্বিতীয় — ditiyô — second.
দ্বিতীয় জামাটা — ditiyô jāmāṭā — the second shirt.
দুই answers how many. দ্বিতীয় (ditiyô) answers which one in the line, and it stands in front of its noun and never changes, the way লাল does. No agreement to learn.
Read the spelling and the romanization again, because they disagree: written দ্ব-, said di-. The cluster is on the page and gone from the mouth.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a promise chapter twelve made

segments.text: Chapter twelve told you two things about the old Sanskrit dv-: that it is gone from the everyday numeral in Bengali, Hindi and Marathi alike, and that it is alive in words borrowed straight back out of Sanskrit. It gave you দ্বার dvār, "door", as its example and left it there.
দ্বিতীয় (ditiyô) is another of those words, and this time it is a number.

utterances: layer: everyday, inherited. two: দুই dui. second: —.
layer: borrowed back from Sanskrit. two: —. second: দ্বিতীয় ditiyô.

segments.text: Bengali keeps two layers of number word. You count in the inherited one; every ordinal in this chapter comes out of the other. That is why none of the five will look much like the numbers you already say.

segments.instruction: dui, then ditiyô
ditiyô jāmāṭā
what is written and what is said — dva on the page, di in the mouth
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what is written and what is said — *dva* on the page, *di* in the mouth]

segments.prompt: Which layer does ditiyo come from, and how can you tell by looking at it?
acceptedResponses: the sanskrit layer, borrowed back; you can tell because the dv- cluster is still written, and chapter twelve said that cluster survives only in re-borrowed words
the sanskrit layer; the dv- is still written
borrowed back from sanskrit, the cluster is on the page

feedback.correct: The cluster is the tell, and you were given it two dozen chapters early.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the first two letters, then remember what chapter twelve said about dv-.

segments.text: How many layers of number word does Bengali keep? (Two.) Which one do you count in? (The inherited one — ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch.) Does দ্বিতীয় (ditiyô) change its ending for the noun? (No — like লাল, it never changes.)
Sources: Wiktionary: দ্বিতীয় (ditiyô).

lessons.title: তৃতীয় (tritiyô) — third, and an ending that now has two members
lessons.gloss: third — the second word to end in -তীয়, which is what makes the ending a shape rather than a coincidence

segments.text: Four recalls, then the second half of a pair.

segments.text: তৃতীয় — tritiyô — third.
তৃতীয় লাল জামাটা — tritiyô lāl jāmāṭā — the third red shirt.
Two adjectives now stand in front of one noun, and neither of them changes. Say তিন, then তৃতীয় (tritiyô): the ত carries over and almost nothing else does.
Same disagreement between page and mouth as last lesson, in a smaller way: the ৃ under the ত is written and the r it stands for is not said.

blocks.title: What you've built: -তীয় is a shape, not a coincidence

segments.text: Set the two side by side and the tails match:

headers: Sanskrit word it was borrowed from
utterances: ordinal: দ্বিতীয় — ditiyô. Sanskrit word it was borrowed from: dvitīya.
ordinal: তৃতীয় — tritiyô. Sanskrit word it was borrowed from: tṛtīya.

segments.text: Wiktionary calls তৃতীয় (tritiyô) a learned borrowing from Sanskrit tṛtīya in those words. Two Sanskrit words ended alike, in -tīya, and the two Bengali words borrowed from them end alike too, in -তীয়.
One word ending a certain way is a fact about that word. Two is a shape, and this is the second — which is why the ending is being named now and was not named last lesson.

segments.instruction: tin, then tritiyô
ditiyô, tritiyô — the pair, back to back
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ditiyô*, *tritiyô* — the pair, back to back]

segments.instruction: tritiyô lāl jāmāṭā

segments.prompt: Which ending do ditiyo and treetiyo share, and where did it come from?
acceptedResponses: -tiyo, from the sanskrit ending -teeya that both source words carried

feedback.correct: Two words, one shape, and the shape is older than Bengali.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the tails of the two words, then look at the Sanskrit column.

segments.text: What is left of তিন inside তৃতীয় (tritiyô)? (The ত.) How many words share the -তীয় ending so far? (Two.) Why was the ending not named one lesson earlier? (One word is not a shape.)
Sources: Wiktionary: তৃতীয় (tritiyô).

lessons.title: চতুর্থ (choturthô) — fourth, on an ending of its own
lessons.gloss: fourth — a different Sanskrit ending, and the only ordinal so far that keeps two pieces of its number

segments.text: Four recalls, then an ordinal that will not join the pair.

segments.instruction: say third, and the ending it shares — R1, one lesson back

segments.text: চতুর্থ — choturthô — fourth.
চতুর্থ নীল জামাটা — choturthô nīl jāmāṭā — the fourth blue shirt.

Say চার, then চতুর্থ (choturthô). Two pieces cross over this time, the চ and the র, which is more of its number than any ordinal you have met keeps. The tail is থ — the letter this book waited longest for, and its second job in five lessons.

blocks.title: What you've built: three endings, and only one of them repeats

segments.text: Samsad's Bengali-English Dictionary gives চতুর্থ (choturthô) its own headword and romanizes it caturtha — the Sanskrit word carried over with nothing altered. Same layer as the last two, different ending:

One member, so this book will not call it a pattern. It is named so you can see that the borrowed layer arrived with more than one shape in it — Sanskrit did not build all its ordinals the same way, and Bengali took them as they were.

segments.instruction: chār, then choturthô
ditiyô, tritiyô, choturthô — two tails, then a third
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ditiyô*, *tritiyô*, *choturthô* — two tails, then a third]

segments.instruction: choturthô nīl jāmāṭā

segments.prompt: Which two pieces of chaar can you still see in choturtho?

feedback.correct: More of its number than any other ordinal here keeps.
feedback.incorrect: Write chaar and choturtho one above the other and compare letter by letter.

segments.text: How many endings have the four ordinals shown so far? (Two — -তীয় twice and -র্থ once.) Which layer are they all from? (The borrowed Sanskrit one.)
Sources: Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, চতুর্থ (choturthô), p. 346 (DSAL).

lessons.title: প্রথম (prothom) — first, and an irregularity Bengali inherited whole
lessons.gloss: first — the one ordinal with no number in it at all, and Bengali did not do that to it

segments.text: Four recalls, then the word with nothing of its number in it.

segments.instruction: say fourth — R1, one lesson back
ask where? — R2, five lessons back
say his, her — R3, twenty lessons back
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: say *his, her* — **R3**, twenty lessons back]

segments.instruction: say black — R4, eighty lessons back

segments.text: প্রথম — prothom — first.
প্রথম কালো জামাটা — prothom kālo jāmāṭā — the first black shirt.
Say এক, then প্রথম (prothom). Not one sound crosses over. তৃতীয় (tritiyô) kept its ত, চতুর্থ (choturthô) kept a চ and a র, and this word keeps nothing.
It carries an everyday second use too: earliest, chief, best — first in the class as much as first in the line.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — nobody in Bengali broke this

segments.text: Wiktionary calls প্রথম (prothom) a learned borrowing from Sanskrit prathama, in the same words it uses for তৃতীয় (tritiyô). So all four ordinals so far come out of the same shelf, and three of them are built on their own Sanskrit number: dvitīya on dvi, tṛtīya on tri, caturtha on catur.

prathama is not built on anything of the kind. Sanskrit's word for one was eka — the word এক still is — and prathama has never shared a sound with it. The gap you are looking at is older than Bengali: Bengali borrowed the word entire, hole and all, and had no hand in making it.
Had this word come first you would have had to take it as a Bengali oddity. Coming fourth, after a shape has held twice and a second ending has appeared once, it can be read for what it is.

segments.instruction: ek, then prothom — and notice nothing carries over
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *ek*, then *prothom* — and notice nothing carries over]

segments.instruction: prothom, ditiyô, tritiyô, choturthô
prothom kālo jāmāṭā

segments.prompt: Did Bengali make prothom unlike ek, or inherit it that way?
acceptedResponses: inherited it that way; sanskrit prathama was already unrelated to sanskrit eka

feedback.correct: The hole is older than the language you are learning.
feedback.incorrect: Sanskrit's one was eka and its first was prathama. Ask which of the two Bengali changed.

segments.text: How much of এক is inside প্রথম (prothom)? (None.) Whose gap is it? (Sanskrit's — Bengali borrowed the word as it stood.) What else can প্রথম (prothom) mean? (Earliest, chief, best.)
Sources: Wiktionary: প্রথম (prothom); Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, প্রথম (prothom), p. 682 (DSAL).

lessons.title: ঞ (nyô) — the nasal of the চ row
lessons.gloss: the nasal of the চ row — the fifth member of a set this book has filled three letters of, and the last letter standing between it and পঞ্চম

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Write চ, জ and ন. Say where each one is made.

segments.instruction: say first — R1, one lesson back
say white — R4, eighty lessons back

segments.text: ঞ (nyô).

Chapter thirty-seven drew a square: ত থ দ ধ, four letters made in one place, sorted by voice and breath. A row of the Bengali grid has a fifth member — a nasal made in that same place. For the teeth row it is ন, and you have been writing it since the first word in this book.
ঞ (nyô) is the fifth member of a different row, the one whose letters are made with the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth:

utterances: the row: voiceless. letters you have: চ chô, ছ chhô.
the row: voiced. letters you have: জ jô.
the row: nasal. letters you have: ঞ nyô.

segments.text: Say চ and then hum through your nose without moving your tongue. That is ঞ (nyô).

You will almost never meet it standing on its own. In modern Bengali it does its work joined to the letter beside it, and the joining you need is ঞ্চ — ঞ (nyô) with চ, the nasal in front of the stop it is made with. That is the next lesson's word.

segments.instruction: ঞ (nyô)

segments.instruction: ঞ্চ
the three nasals this book now has — ন, ঞ (nyô), and the chandrabindu ঁ, which is a nasal with no letter of its own
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the three nasals this book now has — **ন**, **ঞ**, and the chandrabindu **ঁ**, which is a nasal with no letter of its own]

segments.text: Where is ঞ (nyô) made? (Where চ is — the tongue on the roof of the mouth.) What makes it different from চ? (The nose is open.) Which joined form will you need? (ঞ্চ.)
Source: Unicode Bengali chart.

lessons.title: পঞ্চম (ponchom) — fifth, and the two layers touching
lessons.gloss: fifth — the one place in the chapter where you can watch the two layers of number touch, and the moon-dot turn back into a letter

segments.text: পঞ্চম — ponchom — fifth.
পঞ্চম সবুজ জামাটা — ponchom sobuj jāmāṭā — the fifth green shirt.
There is the ঞ্চ you wrote last lesson, between a প and a ম. Its outline is one you already know: প … nasal … চ.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — where পাঁচ came from

segments.text: Samsad's dictionary has the entry this chapter has been building towards. Its headword is পঞ্চ ponchô, glossed five, with পঞ্চম (ponchom) listed under it as fifth. The borrowed layer has its own five, and its fifth is built on it. Put the two fives one above the other:

utterances: layer: borrowed from Sanskrit. five: পঞ্চ — ponchô.
layer: everyday, inherited. five: পাঁচ — pā̃ch.

segments.text: Same প. Same চ. Between them, in the borrowed word a whole letter, ঞ (nyô); in the everyday word the ঁ you were told in chapter twelve was "the chandrabindu, nasalising the vowel".

পাঁচ is পঞ্চ with the nasal letter worn down into a moon-dot, and that is not a guess. Wiktionary's entry for পাঁচ writes its Sanskrit source as পঞ্চ and walks the road between them: pañca, then paṃca, then a Middle Bengali form already spelled with the mark, then পাঁচ. The letter thins to a nasal sign and then to a nasal vowel.

The two layers this chapter opened with are not two vocabularies that happen to sit side by side. In this word you can watch one of them turning into the other, and the whole of the evidence is four letters wide.

segments.instruction: pā̃ch, then ponchô, then ponchom
পঞ্চম (ponchom)
ponchom sobuj jāmāṭā

segments.prompt: What stands in paanch where poncho has the letter nya?

feedback.incorrect: Write the two words one above the other and look at what sits between the pa and the cha.

segments.text: What is পঞ্চম (ponchom) built on? (পঞ্চ, the borrowed five.) And what is পাঁচ? (The same word, worn down.) Which ordinal in this chapter is built on no number at all? (প্রথম (prothom).)
Sources: Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, পঞ্চ, p. 604 (DSAL); Wiktionary: পাঁচ.

segments.text: Read the last row again. Those two are the same word at two ends of a long road, and the difference between them is a letter you learned two lessons ago turning into a mark you learned in chapter twelve.
The chapter cost exactly one new letter, ঞ (nyô), and spent it on the row that proves the point.

Which layer are all five ordinals from? (The borrowed Sanskrit one.) Which of them has no number inside it at all? (প্রথম (prothom) — and the gap is Sanskrit's, not Bengali's.) Which two rows of the table are the same word? (পাঁচ and পঞ্চ.)
